texts.label: text
texts.orig: The paper deals with the problem of automatic speaker change detection: A metric-based algorithm; called MDISTBIC, which means Modified DISTBIC, is proposed in this paper: The algorithm originates from the DISTBIC algorithm and modifies it in order to reach higher efliciency. Both the DISTBIC and the MDISTBIC methods are tested in a number of experiments As the results show; the MDISTBIC algorithm is more efficient than the DISTBIC algorithm in a majority of tests.

texts.orig: There are three main speaker change detection approaches determined as the moments in which a distance measure computed between two adjacent windows shifted the speech signal reaches a local maximum. In the model-based approach it is assumed that a model of each speaker the voice of which is contained in an utterance has been trained before the speaker change detection algorithm starts The speaker changes are then detected as the instants when it is necessary to change the speaker model in order it match the speech signal. The last approach is the decoder-guided approach. Here, the speaker changes are determined according to information provided by speech recognition system which decodes the spoken audio along stream at first (e.g.  possible speaker changes are at every silence location)

texts.orig: The first step relies on distance-based segmentation defined from the likelihoods of adjacent windows. In each window; the data are assumed to result from single multi-dimensional Gaussian process. The question is, whether the data from the two adjacent windows together fit better with single multidimensional Gaussian or whether a two-window representation justifies the data better: In order to answer this question, the Kullback-Leibler distance can be used for example.
